I’ve been splitting Google Search Console queries by word count lately to see how the mix of searches we appear for is changing.
 
Here are the custom regex filters I use:
 
1 word
^\S+$
 
2–4 words
^(\S+\s+){1,3}\S+$
 
5–10 words
^(\S+\s+){4,9}\S+$
 
11–20 words
^(\S+\s+){10,19}\S+$
 
21+ words
^(\S+\s+){20,}\S+$
 
And for queries that start like questions:
 
^(who|what|when|where|why|how|which|can|does|do|is|are|should|will)\b
 
You can paste these into GSC under Query → Custom (regex), then export each group and analyze them with AI.
 
Why?
 
Because a 2-word query and a 20-word query usually represent very different searches.
 
Shorter queries tend to be categories, products, brands, or broad topics.
 
As queries get longer, you start seeing much more context like use cases, constraints, comparisons, problems, and full questions that sound surprisingly similar to what buyers ask on sales calls.
 
That makes the YoY comparison interesting too.
 
In the image, my client is now getting nearly 25× more impressions from 11–20-word queries than at the same point last year. (yes, I know, ZERO clicks  👁️)
 
And no, these don’t seem to be weird AI-looking strings. They’re searches like:
 
“which [insert SaaS category] products in the united states come with licenses and regulatory compliance?”
 
That gives me a quick way to isolate the most specific searches and look for content opportunities inside them.
 
If Google is already showing one of my pages for a 17-word question I only answer indirectly, that’s a pretty good clue that I should probably answer it properly.
 
And if the same question keeps showing up in sales calls? Even better.

I analyzed Google Search Console data from several B2B SaaS websites and found a few clear patterns. (Blog on this in the first comment.)

As queries get longer, they contain more context and start to sound more like the questions buyers ask on sales calls.

You can almost see the searcher adding context.

2–4 words: they name the category.
“lending software” > They know what type of product they’re looking for, but they haven’t given Google much context yet.

5–10 words: they describe the need.
“field service software for a small roofing crew” > Now the search includes a use case, audience, workflow, or problem.

11–20 words: they ask a real buyer question.
“which lending platform handles origination, servicing, and syndication in one system?” > These are the queries that start sounding a lot like questions prospects ask during demos and sales calls.

Then at 21+ words, the pattern gets harder to interpret.

Some of these may be human searches, but many look suspiciously like AI query fan-outs: long, highly specific searches generated behind the scenes when an AI system breaks a larger question into smaller searches.

And this is where the pattern gets more interesting.

The more context the query contains, the fewer clicks it tends to generate.

In the shortest searches, only about 2% were questions.
In the longest searches, about 97% were questions.

But as queries got longer, clicks collapsed.

Across the data:

> 1–2 words generated about 1.9 clicks per 100 impressions
> 3–4 words dropped to about 0.3 clicks per 100 impressions
> 5+ word searches moved toward almost no clicks at all

So here’s what the data actually shows:

Longer queries are more question-like, more specific, and much less likely to generate a website visit.

My interpretation is that there may be two different behaviors inside that pattern:

As human searches get longer, they become more specific and conversational.

Then at the very long end, some of those searches may be coming from AI systems doing research on the buyer’s behalf.

That creates a pretty important problem for B2B SaaS content.

The queries that tell us the most about what the buyer needs may also be the queries least likely to send that buyer to our website.

So my next step is to test this against something much closer to the buyer.

I’m going to cross these GSC queries with the actual questions prospects ask during demos and sales calls.

I want to see how closely the 11–20+ word queries match real buyer questions, and if the 21+ word queries look meaningfully different.

That should help answer two questions:

Which searches reflect real buyer demand?
And which ones are probably AI looking for information to answer that buyer?

If buyers and AI are both searching, we need to know what each is looking for before we decide where to put our content effort.

I’ll share what I find once I’ve compared the two.

posts.content:
It took me ~15 minutes to build this month's GEO plan for a client. P.S.: What could I have done differently here? any tips?  👁️ 

  🤖  1.     I pulled 30 recorded sales calls

  🤖  2.     I gave the transcripts to Claude and asked it to pull out the questions prospects asked, in the words they used

It filtered out demo questions, scheduling questions, and other noise, and left me with roughly 50 real buyer questions.

  🤖  3.     Then I tested every question across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, and Google AI Mode. I used temporary or incognito sessions where possible to reduce personalization from my own search history.

For each one, I wanted to know:

Are we being cited?
Are we being recommended?
Or are we completely missing from the answer?

Ahrefs Brand Radar can automate a lot of this, and I love it, but it’s expensive. If you have the budget, use it, I find it better than Semrush's AI tracking features.

The manual check still gave me something useful very quickly.

Turns out my client is showing up well for TOFU searches where people already understood the category. But we're much weaker on pain-related questions, those questions people ask when they know they have a problem, but they don’t know what kind of solution they need yet.

So if someone already knows the category, we have a good chance of showing up.
If they’re still trying to understand what’s causing their problem or what they should even do about it, we’re much harder to find.

That gave me a very obvious content gap.

  🤖  4.     I asked Claude to build a plan around the gaps.

It prioritized questions where:

> we weren’t showing up
> the buyer intent was strong
> and the topic was relevant to what my client sells

Those went to the top of the list.

  🤖  5.     Within 5 minutes, I was already updating existing content and had a month-long GEO optimization plan that could run alongside the content calendar I already had.

The biggest takeaway for me was where the strategy started.

It started with real questions from real prospects. If Sales hadn’t given me access to those call recordings, I probably would’ve built the plan around keyword data, competitor content, or questions that AI thought buyers might ask.

Those can all be useful inputs, but the sales calls showed me the exact language prospects were already using while evaluating the problem.

That made the rest of the GEO work much easier to prioritize.

One of the easiest ways to underestimate AI search is to look at your AI referral traffic isolated.

If you open GA4 and see that ChatGPT sent 40 visits and Google sent 40,000, naturally, AI looks almost irrelevant.

But Similarweb followed what happened after people received brand recommendations from ChatGPT and found that only 8.8% of AI-influenced visits arrived as recognizable AI traffic, while 55.9% arrived through search.

That’s because someone can ask AI “What’s the best software for X?” --

then

>    AI mentions your company 
>    the person closes the tool and keeps working 
>    a few days later, they remember your name and Google you 
>    GA4 sees organic traffic, Google Search Console sees the branded search and click…

…and neither one can tell you that ChatGPT introduced the company in the first place.

That’s why looking only at chatgpt . com / referral can give you a very incomplete picture.

AI referral traffic can tell you how many people clicked directly from an AI tool, but it can't really show you everyone who discovered your company through AI and came back later through Google, direct traffic, paid, or another channel.

That group could be much larger than the referral number tell.

If you’re trying to understand how much AI search matters for your SaaS company, don’t judge it from referral traffic alone.

Also look at whether branded and direct search is growing, ask leads how they first heard about you, and check if your company appears when buyers ask AI the questions that matter in your category.

posts.content:
Years of living and breathing SEO and leading SEO departments for different agencies made me fluent in keywords, algorithms, and schema. I thought I knew “organic search.”

Then 5 years ago a friend asked me to write on one of her clients' website.

"Easy!", I thought. 3,000 keyword-stuffed words, done.

𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐠𝐢𝐠 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐦𝐲 𝐒𝐄𝐎 𝐛𝐮𝐛𝐛𝐥𝐞. It turned into my biggest wake-up call. My own aha moment in my career.

Suddenly organic search felt bigger than rankings and keywords. SEO wasn't the center of the world.

And I realized that expertise can become a tunnel if you never poke your head out. 💀 

Writing forced me to zoom out. Same landscape, but new lens.

Along the way, I had to unlearn everything that kept me stuck in the weeds:

- 𝐊𝐞𝐲𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐬 < 𝐦𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠.
Ranking words in an H1 is easy; speaking your buyer’s language is what resonates.

- 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐥𝐬𝐞.
Product-update posts and release notes won’t bring a lot of traffic, so legacy SEOs don't prioritize. But they’re exactly what high intent potential customers read.

- 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐭 𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡.
Real strategy revisits, refreshes, and repurposes as the product evolves.

- 𝐀𝐧 𝐚𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 ≠ 𝐦𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐦.
Page speed and internal links remove friction but they don’t create momentum on their own. Story, clarity, messaging, and a strong point of view do that.

- 𝐑𝐚𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 ≠ 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐬.
Number 1 rankings on the SERP can bring prospects to the door, but only your messaging gets them to pull up a chair. That’s where business happens.

If you've been considering learning a new skill, this is your sign.

I encourage you to be a V-shaped professional. Grow your wings. Challenge yourself. Watch what happens.

What do marketing and being chased by a lion have in common? 𝐍𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭-𝐨𝐫-𝐟𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐞.

Tight deadlines, performance pressure, juggling a million things at once, Google updates... 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠. 𝐈𝐬. 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐟𝐮𝐥.

In fact, 80% of marketers report feeling overworked.

So how do you remind your nervous system that you’re at work, not in the Discovery Channel? Here's what works for me: 

𝟏. 𝐓𝐨𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐬. 𝐍𝐨, 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐥𝐲, 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐬. Go outside. Feel the sun. Breathe actual air. Your brain wasn’t designed to stare at a glowing rectangle all day. Nature is magical and can help ease your mind during anxiety episodes. Don't be afraid to stop working if you body truly needs it. 

𝟐. 𝐓𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐟𝐞𝐰 𝐝𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐚 𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞. Lock hours on your calendar for specific tasks and commit to completing them in that timeframe. No cheating. Be honest with yourself. Set a timer, commit to the task, and get it done. Future you will thank you.

𝟑. 𝐄𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐠. 𝐑𝐢𝐩 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐢𝐝. 𝐃𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐬𝐤 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚𝐯𝐨𝐢𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐫. Got one report that's freaking you out? Start working on it first and early in your day. Your brain will fight you at first, but once you tackle that task, everything else feels easier. You're at your job because you have the skills and expertise to do it. It may take a while to master this but once you start eating the frog first, you'll rewire your brain and anxiety inducing tasks will be easier to tackle. 

This of course works for me and may not work for everybody. Also, full disclosure: I am not recommending eating actual frogs. 🐸

To all my friends in Marketing, I feel you. 

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐱𝐢𝐞𝐭𝐲-𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐣𝐨𝐛𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞, but it’s also one of the most rewarding. Because we care. We’re passionate. We love what we do.

So if you’re feeling anxious about a client call, a deadline, or AI taking over organic search (lol), remember this: stress and anxiety doesn’t define your worth.

Marketing is tough, but so are we. 💪

Some people prefer quick huddles over text. Others want everything in writing, clear and direct. There’s no one-size-fits-all rule.

At the end of the day, we’re human. Let’s not lose the human touch or bash someone for simply trying their best to improve communication with their team.

I asked ChatGPT how I can get LLMs (Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT) to recommend my product or service to its users. Here's what it told me:

1. "𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐭: Write blogs, whitepapers, and case studies showcasing your product's ability to solve specific problems. Ensure these are hosted on your website and 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐬." 

👉  AI loves crawling authoritative websites like Forbes, Harvard Business Review, Entrepreneur, Gartner, Medium, GlobeNewswire, Business Wire, and LinkedIn to train its datasets. If you can afford guest posts or mentions on these platforms, or any relevant website in your industry, go for it. That’s where the bots are training!

In the meantime, focus on your own content. Highlight your software’s features, solutions, use cases, and real-world success stories. Think blogs, whitepapers, and customer case studies.

2. "𝐄𝐧𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐋𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: Ensure your product is listed on high-profile marketplaces or directories like G2, Capterra, or industry-specific directories. Include detailed descriptions and customer reviews." 

👉 Get profiles on all the key review platforms: G2, Capterra, SaaStr, TrustRadius, and pack them with details. Show off features, use cases, and success stories, but most importantly get real client reviews. Lots of them. Reviews are gold, not just for leads but now for AI.

3. "𝐈𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐒𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐚 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐮𝐩: Use structured data (e.g., FAQ, product, and review schema) on your website. This makes your product's information more accessible and easier for search engines and AI to process." 

👉 Not much to say here. I think we all know structured data does wonders for SEO. But hey, If AI is asking for it, why not give it what it wants?

4. "𝐒𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬: Publish content demonstrating how your product solves the exact problem users are likely to query about. Include detailed use cases, testimonials, and metrics." 

👉 Right? Because if you want AI to know what your product does and what needs it solves, you need to tell it somehow. Metrics, case studies, testimonials, they all help tell your story.

5. "𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐅𝐀𝐐𝐬: Submit FAQ-style content to platforms where your target audience might search for recommendations, such as Quora, Reddit, or niche forums." 

👉 This is a good one. You need to anticipate the questions your ICP is asking (ask your sales people), find out where they're hanging out (their watering holes), and be there ready to answer them. Your FAQ page? It's training data for AI.

𝐐𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝟐𝟎𝟏𝟎 𝐒𝐄𝐎, 𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭? 🙃 🫠

𝐇𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐞𝐬? 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐠𝐨? 𝐆𝐨𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞? 𝐈’𝐦 𝐚𝐥𝐰𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞.

Last week, during a feedback session, one of my CMOs hit me with this: "A siloed specialist isn’t enough." And she’s absolutely right. (The famous 𝐓 𝐨𝐫 𝐕-𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐝 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐫 buzzword, everyone.) But what does this mean for SEOs?

Special thanks to Cecilia Pérez-Muskus for the food for thought! 👏 

We already know the "nice-to-haves" for SEOs: some UX, some paid media, pretending to know Photoshop (Canva is my limit, tbh). But what about the big, complex, "sit-at-the-leadership-table" kind of skills? You know, the ones typically reserved for CMOs?

Here’s what I mean:

1️⃣ 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐎𝐈 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠

“We ranked #1 for X keyword!” doesn’t hit the same when leadership asks, “Cool, but how does that make us money?” SEOs who can connect rankings to revenue, CAC, LTV, and ROI? That’s how you go from a simple SEO to a growth-driving marketer.

2️⃣ 𝐁𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠

SEO shouldn't be just keywords and traffic. SEOs should be helping their brands stand out. If you don’t deeply understand your brand’s UVP and audience, you’re just chasing vanity metrics. You want to create content that says, “This is who we are, and this is why you need us,” not “Look at all this random traffic we got! Let's crelebrate we're ranking for 'what is project management'” 🥴

3️⃣ 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚-𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Advanced analytics shouldn't be just for your data team. SEOs need to own their numbers and prove how they influence the entire customer journey. Why? Because “We drove more traffic” won’t unlock a bigger budget, but “Here’s how we contributed to pipeline revenue” just might.

𝐀𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐠𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐲𝐨𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐄𝐎, 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐥𝐲. 𝐈𝐭’𝐬 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐞𝐚𝐦.

Wouldn’t it be amazing if your SEOs actually understood this stuff? Or are we just throwing them into the silo and hoping for the best?

More importantly: Are you investing in the growth of your specialists? Or are we still in the “just rank #1 and we’re good” phase of 2010?

𝐏.𝐒. 𝐀𝐥𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰, 𝐈’𝐯𝐞 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐠. 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞’𝐬 𝐚 𝐤𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐞 𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐓 𝐨𝐫 𝐕-𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐝, 𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐝𝐫𝐨𝐩 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬. 𝐈’𝐝 𝐥𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 𝐢𝐭 𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐦𝐲 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬.

I promised myself this a few years ago after one of the worst experiences with a manager.

I had a trip planned halfway across the world. I’d be working in European time while they were on Mountain Time. Every deadline was met, every meeting attended, and not a single project fell through the cracks.

But was that good enough for them? Nope. They told me I had to work their schedule. And if that wasn’t hard enough (there was a 9-hour difference), they added, “Since you’re traveling, you should probably work double to make up for it.” 😳

To this day, I remember how that made me feel: insulted, demoralized, and undervalued. And I promised myself right then and there that I’d never manage that way.

It’s time to redefine what great management looks like, especially in a remote-friendly industry like marketing, because let’s be honest, “work double because you’re traveling” isn’t it.

What’s your take on this? How do you balance flexibility with accountability in your leadership style?

Women-led leadership IS different, and that’s okay. 

𝐌𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐥𝐲, 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐛𝐞 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐞𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞.

Women lead differently. Emotional intelligence, collaboration, and long-term thinking is a priority for us. It happens at every level. Do not expect us to conform to a traditional, results-at-all-costs leadership style.

𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐚 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞?

Instead of debating if men or women lead better, maybe we should be debating how to create space for different leadership styles to thrive.

A hot topic this week with some clients has been data from SEO tools such as Ahrefs, SEMRush and others... 

Most SEO tools work on assumptions and estimates. They show traffic numbers, keyword volumes, and rankings, but it’s all approximate and usually based on some rather bold assumptions. 

Trusting those numbers blindly can leave you with the wrong impression about how your site is performing or even how your competitors are doing. 

The only place to get the real data? Google Search Console.

It tells you exactly what people search to find your site. Shows real clicks, impressions, and rankings straight from Google. No guesswork. Just facts.

SEO tools can give you ideas. Google Search Console gives you clarity.

If you’re relying purely on third-party tools, you might be missing the bigger picture.  

This is where the knowledge of a good SEO is worth their weight in gold, they know which data points matter, and how to interpret them - it's not guesswork - it's years of honing their skills to know what to read from data.

I don’t think I’ve talked to a single person in the last year that’s seeing growth from organic search. 

No exaggeration.

Everyone I talk to is seeing flat or declining traffic from search. 

Why are we not talking more about this??!

I talked to a founder recently who’s always been bullish on SEO. The type who never accepted “seasonality” or “it’s the algorithm” as an excuse for organic declines.

Even he said they’ve given up on it.

He’s the minority. Most leaders I talk to are seeing the same thing but still pouring time, money, and headcount into it.

What are we doing? 

Here’s my take on why teams are still investing in something that’s not working / showing diminishing returns: 

1️⃣ They’ve invested too much to stop.
There are full-time roles, team structures, tooling, workflows all built around a channel that used to work. Walking away feels too expensive.

2️⃣ They don’t know what else to do.
Search has been the go-to growth engine for over a decade. When it stalls, the fallback options feel riskier (and pricier): paid search, paid social, brand campaigns, etc.

3️⃣ They think it’s a skill gap and not a system problem.
Some teams still believe they just need to tweak something. Make a change in marketing leadership. Hire the right SEO lead. Refresh content. Find the unlock. But what if the channel itself has fundamentally changed?

I don’t think things are going to get better. But that doesn’t mean we’re screwed. 

The teams that thrive next won’t be the ones chasing channels. They’ll be the ones willing to pause, ask better questions, and start from within.

For true content brands, that’s always been the play.

The channels come and go. Their perspective is what endures.

I’ve been splitting Google Search Console queries by word count lately to see how the mix of searches we appear for is changing.
 
Here are the custom regex filters I use:
 
1 word
^\S+$
 
2–4 words
^(\S+\s+){1,3}\S+$
 
5–10 words
^(\S+\s+){4,9}\S+$
 
11–20 words
^(\S+\s+){10,19}\S+$
 
21+ words
^(\S+\s+){20,}\S+$
 
And for queries that start like questions:
 
^(who|what|when|where|why|how|which|can|does|do|is|are|should|will)\b
 
You can paste these into GSC under Query → Custom (regex), then export each group and analyze them with AI.
 
Why?
 
Because a 2-word query and a 20-word query usually represent very different searches.
 
Shorter queries tend to be categories, products, brands, or broad topics.
 
As queries get longer, you start seeing much more context like use cases, constraints, comparisons, problems, and full questions that sound surprisingly similar to what buyers ask on sales calls.
 
That makes the YoY comparison interesting too.
 
In the image, my client is now getting nearly 25× more impressions from 11–20-word queries than at the same point last year. (yes, I know, ZERO clicks  👁️)
 
And no, these don’t seem to be weird AI-looking strings. They’re searches like:
 
“which [insert SaaS category] products in the united states come with licenses and regulatory compliance?”
 
That gives me a quick way to isolate the most specific searches and look for content opportunities inside them.
 
If Google is already showing one of my pages for a 17-word question I only answer indirectly, that’s a pretty good clue that I should probably answer it properly.
 
And if the same question keeps showing up in sales calls? Even better.
